Finally, the country of study location signiﬁcantly moderated the
association between self-reports and objective measures, Qvalue
(6) ¼ 32.18, p < .001.12 Across the 15 studies included in the
analysis, ﬁve studies are from Latin America (namely, Mexico and
Bolivia). Comparing the effect sizes between these two categories
of countries reveals that the average of the 12 association values
from non-Latin American countries (r ¼ .45) is higher than the
average of the seven association values from the Latin American
countries (r ¼ .36).

Main study: spatial positioning
For each family, we then examined the ﬁrst 60 images in Google
using ‘‘the Simpsons”, ‘‘the Flintstones”, and ‘‘the Addams” as key
words. We simply recorded the number of times in which the male
vs. the female of each couple occupied the left position (from the
perspective of the observer).
Overall, males were positioned to the left in 60% of all images,
which deviates reliably from chance, binomial test p = .008, there-
by conﬁrming our ﬁrst hypothesis. However, looking separately at
the families, this was entirely due to the Addams family where the

the SD composite alone, accounted for 34% of the variance,
F(22,462) = 84.21, p < .01. During the fourth step when the SR com-

During the model 2 analysis of GPA, the step one and step two
regressions revealed identical non-signiﬁcant effects of back-
ground variables to model 1. The third step analysis, which tested
the SR composite alone, accounted for 64% of the variance in GPA,
F(22,462) = 280.05, p < .01. The fourth step of the analysis (in
which the SR composite was entered along with the SD composite)
accounted for 69% of the variance in GPA, F(23,461) = 261.56,
p < .01. The change between these two steps was a 5% improve-
ment in prediction of GPA variance. Thus, the inclusion of the SD
composite increased the size of the prediction by 5% when com-
pared to the SR composite alone.
Regarding VSOL, the ﬁrst hierarchical regression tested model 1
(in which the SD composite alone was entered in the third step).

(self-alone low beneﬁt vs. self-alone high beneﬁt vs. self-and-
friend beneﬁt vs. self-and-other beneﬁt vs. other-alone beneﬁt)
on rates of over-reporting performance was signiﬁcant, v2(4) = 12.76,
p = .02. Hypothesis 2 posited that people would act dishonestly
more frequently when the beneﬁts of doing so were split equally
between themselves and another person than when they accrued
all of the beneﬁts. Supporting this hypothesis, participants in the
self-and-friend beneﬁt condition were twice as likely to report
solving the unsolvable word jumble (43%) than were participants
in the self-alone high beneﬁt condition, 21%, v2(1) = 6.81, p = .01.
Participants in the self-and-other beneﬁt condition were also more
likely to report solving the unsolvable word jumble (37%) than
were participants in the self-alone high beneﬁt condition, 21%,
v2(1) = 3.88, p = .05.
Results supported the notion that participants would be most
likely to cheat when they had both a personal ﬁnancial stake in
the outcome and could beneﬁt someone else by overstating their
performance. Speciﬁcally, participants in the self-and-other high
beneﬁt condition cheated signiﬁcantly more often (37%) than did
those in the other-alone beneﬁts condition, 16%, v2(1) = 5.59,
